hints: Focus on the reaction type here, hydroxide replacing bromide on a primary halogenoalkane is nucleophilic substitution.
Spot your players, the $\text{OH}^-$ ion is the electron-rich nucleophile and the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ bonded to Br is the electron-poor electrophile.
Remember curly arrows always show an electron pair moving from rich to poor, and the $\text{C-Br}$ bond must break to give $\text{Br}^-$.
walkthrough:
**Identify the mechanism type**

This is nucleophilic substitution of a primary bromoalkane by aqueous hydroxide. Think nucleophile attacks, leaving group leaves.

Overall reaction:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Find the nucleophile and electrophile**

The $\text{OH}^-$ ion has full lone pairs, so it is electron rich and loves positive centres. The C attached to Br is $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ because Br is more electronegative and pulls the bonding electrons away, so it is electron poor.

**Draw the correct curly arrows**

A curly arrow must start at the source of electrons and point to where they go. So one arrow starts from a lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ atom to make the new C-O bond. At the same time, the $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair moves onto Br to form $\text{Br}^-$. This is heterolytic fission, not homolytic.

options.A: Correct. The lone pair on the nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$ attacks the electrophilic $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. This is the proper direction for a curly arrow, from electron-rich to electron-poor, to start the SN2 step.
options.B: Incorrect. Curly arrows show electron movement, they never start from a $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ atom which is electron poor. This reverses the logic and is a common arrow-direction trap.
options.C: Incorrect. The $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair must move away from carbon onto Br to make $\text{Br}^-$. Drawing it back onto C would wrongly keep the electrons on carbon.
options.D: Incorrect. This is nucleophilic substitution by heterolytic fission to give ions ($\text{Br}^-$), not homolytic fission to give radicals. Homolytic fission with single-headed fishhook arrows belongs to free radical mechanisms.
